records.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts (execution 148.378, 1 of 8 correct) failed the same way as prior rounds: every losing run did split the sum-shown/product-shown cases and enumerate pairs, but judged "does not know" against the public number alone, declared both branches contradictory, then committed to a plausible-looking pair anyway; two hit the token cap looping. That is exactly what the incumbent's private-value grouping clause targets, and rounds 10, 14, 16 and 18 all tried making that clause more executable and lost held-out every time, so re-testing it is not worthwhile. I therefore submit a strictly lossless compression instead: the only change is deleting two definite articles ("the public statements", "the announcements"). Every content word, clause and step order is byte-identical, so transfer should be unchanged while 73 tokens wins a held-out tie.

Fresh rollouts (148.379) scored 8/8, so training is saturated and only transfer matters. All eight took the vague 'characterize the locus' branch into theta-parametrization and parameter elimination; the two costliest traces (15843 and 12344 tokens) burned thousands of tokens doubting whether their unnormalized quadratic was an ellipse or a circle, while the cheapest clean traces just evaluated explicit roots and read off the centre. Only one of eight traces ever mentioned exceptional values, so that clause is inert tax. This edit spends the same 70 tokens to replace the vague branch and the inert clause with one executable move plus the Mobius circle-preservation fact that removes the ellipse-versus-circle stall, which should transfer to any locus-of-roots problem.

Rollouts scored 4/8. All four failures burned the full 16384-token budget; three never closed the reasoning block and the fourth closed but was truncated before any box. Yet every failure already held the correct exact value by 8-10 percent of its trace and then restated it 15-27 more times while opening 24-37 'Alternatively' and 64-74 'Wait' branches, so the loss is pure non-termination, not method. The incumbent's close trigger, 'one exact value plus one confirming check', names no event the student can observe, and the four successes closed only after repeating the value many times. I replaced just that trigger with a countable event the student demonstrably generates on any problem - the third restatement of the same exact value - leaving every other clause byte-identical at 166 tokens versus the incumbent's 169.

Fresh rollouts (148.381) scored 6/8; both misses reported a single factor. One assumed the whole run came from one polynomial and stopped at its degree cap; the other differenced across polynomials, concluded each serves exactly one input, and stopped at the menu size. The incumbent's prohibition 'never reporting one factor alone' sits right where both failed and neither rollout acted on it, while all six successes explicitly performed the per-polynomial accumulation. So I replaced that ignored negative clause with the positive executable arithmetic it was gesturing at - add deg P once for every polynomial on the menu - which names the exact combining step and should transfer to any bounded-capacity-times-number-of-objects counting problem. Net slightly shorter than the incumbent.

Round 19 fell to 3/8 and four of the five failures ran the 16384-token cap dead; one of those had already derived and boxed a correct value inside its reasoning, then restarted a fresh write-up and was cut off mid-sentence. The three others never closed reasoning at all, re-deriving the same constants and second-guessing correct algebra dozens of times. Length exhaustion has been the dominant failure in almost every round of this hint's history, yet no prior edit targeted it. Meanwhile 'a zero or impossible intermediate means relabel, not restart' is provably inert: neither word appears in any of the eight rollouts. So that clause is replaced by an explicit commit-and-stop trigger, which is shorter than the incumbent and should curb runaway rollouts on unseen questions too.

All 8 rollouts failed (0/8) with the same error: each priced the event by dividing one by a count of orders (1/4 seven times, plus 1/24, 1/16, 1/2), asserting a random permutation of bags. Clause grep shows the incumbent's standalone anti-uniform warning is executed 0/8 (red-flag 0/8, unreachable 0/8, admissible-word 0/8) while its setup and one-half clauses are used 8/8, so the warning is inert text the student reads past. This edit fuses the prohibition into the pricing directive itself - walk each qualifying run move by move and multiply step probabilities, never divide one by a count of orders or runs - so the ban arrives attached to the action it governs instead of as a separate slogan, and lands at 163 tokens versus the incumbent's 176.

Seven of eight rollouts hit the 16384-token cap. Most did build the small-size tables the hint asks for and got correct entries, then set up a competing symbolic model, saw it disagree with those entries, and spent the remaining budget hunting the discrepancy and swapping models rather than trusting the recorded numbers. The one correct rollout differed mainly by letting its table settle the clash and moving on. So the absolute ban 'never leave the table for theory', which no rollout obeys, becomes a precedence rule the student can execute mid-conflict; every step the winning rollout used is preserved and the hint is one token shorter than the incumbent.

Fresh rollouts scored 5/8. All eight reached the gcd and tabulated every divisor candidate, including the right one, so that machinery is load-bearing; all three failures then abandoned their own table and overrode it with a plausibility argument built on the stated grouping count. The incumbent's grouping clause targets exactly that error and prevented none of the three, and no rollout used it; 'substitute numbers only at the end' was again executed zero of eight times, as in rounds 10, 11 and 15. Adding a selection or tiebreak rule has lost held-out here four times (rounds 2, 6, 7, 17), so instead this deletes both inert clauses and spends the tokens on the two executable arithmetic moves that co-occurred with this slot's best-ever held-out: naming the base a percent multiplies, and summing parts before a single division. It is shorter than the incumbent.

Five of eight rollouts failed and the shared cause was never pinning the reflection constant s: four ran to the 16384-token cap philosophising about what the involution means, and the ones that did commit guessed s by trial instead of deriving it, while all three winners got s in one line from the two supplied constant terms and finished early. The incumbent's 'fix s from the given values at x = 0' told them where to look but not what to compute, so I replaced it with the explicit one-line formula s = f(0) + g(0); that is a concrete first move that should transfer to any unseen problem where two objects are tied by a constant-sum symmetry. I also dropped the now-redundant 'match constant terms, then look for a shared symmetry' clause, whose job the explicit formula absorbs, keeping the hint one token shorter than the incumbent.

1/8 correct. Seven of eight rollouts did write small cases out literally, so the incumbent's core step fires, but every failure then produced a structural/permutation argument that contradicted its own written case and spent the rest of the 16384-token budget relitigating which was right, oscillating between rival exponents and mostly never boxing anything. The incumbent's removed qualifier 'not arguing abstractly' is inert - the students argue abstractly anyway, after measuring - so I spend those tokens on a precedence rule that resolves the deadlock in one move: the written value wins, so advance instead of relitigating. This should transfer to any tabulate-and-fit problem where a tempting shortcut collides with measured data, and it is 3 tokens shorter than the incumbent.
